#3287. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website.

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

#3286. ‘Scrubs’ Star Sarah Chalke On J.D. & Elliot’s Big Reveal & Surprise Twist, Sean & Charlie’s Quick Exit, Ollie’s Arrival & What Comes Next

SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 207 of ABC’s Scrubs “My Story.”

Episode 207 of ABC’s Scrubs revival gave fans answers about what led to J.D. (Zach Braff) and Elliot’s (Sarah Chalke) shocking divorce, it gave them a glimpse at what a romantic reconciliation may look like and it gave them hope that the former couple may get back together.

J.D. and Elliot — both single again after their recent flames Charlie (Rachel Bilson) and Sean (Scott Foley) fell for each other — gave their son Ollie (Kellan Tetlow) a version of the talk before J.D. invited his ex to dinner via text to celebrate how well they did as co-parents. Related Stories Politics Midterm Elections: Piers Morgan & Rashida Jones On How 'Uncensored's Going Into Uncharted Territory Tonight, The Trump Wild Card Legal Attorney For CNN, MS NOW & Politico Talks About Why It's Urgent To Stop Latest Trump White House Ban: "The Chilling Effect Is Immense"

“Why didn’t we work, we should’ve worked,” J.D. said at the dinner, speaking for all Scrubs fans. The two went on to lift the veil on how they went from the happy couple seen sharing many milestones together in the original series’ Season 8 finale flashforward to exes and why Elliot pulled the trigger on a divorce.

J.D. and Elliot continued the conversation outside where, walking by a waterfront, J.D. professed his love and the two kissed. Moments later, it turned out that J.D. had imagined the date while keeping company of a hallucinating elderly dementia patient who thinks she is lying on the ceiling.

In a video interview with Deadline, Chalke discussed the J.D.-Elliot scene and its twist, the challenges of filming the kissing scene in a public space, crafting the episode’s elaborate fantasy sequences, that ambiguous glance J.D. and Elliot exchanged at the very end of the episode as well as Elliot and Sean’s short-lived re-coupling.

Chalke didn’t find out about the J.D.-Elliot fantasy date idea until a few episodes into production on Season 2 when it was pitched to her by series showrunner Aseem Batra.

“I was like, oh my gosh, it’s incredible, I love that we were exploring it,” Chalke said. “I think they really listened to a lot of the fan reactions from Episode 1 of the revival, and everybody was asking, okay, J.D. and Elliot, tell us more about that. Why didn’t it work out, what happened, what went wrong?”

The revival’s first episode, which marked J.D.’s return to Sacred Heart, delivered the bombshell that he and Elliot are divorced without much of an explanation.

“I thought this was the most brilliant way in; I love episodes like this, they’re my favorite ones of Scrubs where you have a misdirect and think you’re getting one thing and then you get this curveball at the end,” Chalke said. “I thought this way in of J.D. having the dementia patient and then having her up on the ceiling, he goes to join her on the ceiling to comfort her and then goes into his own fantasy, I thought it was such a cool way for us to end up finding out more about their relationship and what went wrong and what went right.”

“We really haven’t gotten into it,” Chalke said about the reason for J.D. and Elliot’s divorce. “We got a taste of it in the revival Season 1 in Episode 3 where they’re in the bathroom together, Elliot is crying, and they’re like, I don’t know how to do this, who are we actually going to be to each other in this new life where we’re working together and co-parenting?”

In that Season 1 scene, J.D. and Elliot ultimately agree that they would figure out what the next phase of their relationship is because they will always be family.

During Elliot and J.D.’s restaurant date in Episode 207, we finally got the backstory of their separation.

“Now we find out that J.D. actually was just trying to do the right thing and thought he was doing the right thing for their marriage and for their relationship and for their family to go out and become a concierge doctor, and in doing so lost all of himself and who he felt like who he was, and wasn’t open to talking about it with Elliot,” Chalke said. “She felt like, okay, you shut me out, and that was the gap. I loved that the writers had Elliot say, I could have been there for you, this is what I promised you, I could have done this, it could have been different. I liked it because I feel like you really see both sides. You understand these are two human beings that were just doing their best, and I thought it was such a cool twist to have J.D. say ‘I can’t fully be myself without you,’ and then make the decision for Elliot not to tell her, like actually for her. I thought that was beautiful to say, I can’t do this to her, we don’t know if it’ll work out. I can’t risk hurting her again.”

Even in his own fantasy, while J.D. is all in, telling Elliot that “I don’t think I can ever really be myself without you,” she is pushing back, pointing out that “we can’t do this” and “every time we try it, it ends badly.”

Chalke is happy that Elliot didn’t get swept up in the moment and kept it real.

“I think first of all, it was really important to the writers that the mislead works, and that the audience doesn’t know that this is a fantasy,” she said. “I think for Elliot, this was obviously, without saying, the most significant relationship of her lifetime. It was so painful to her that it didn’t work out, and I think that she absolutely has her walls up of like, well, we can’t do that again because that didn’t work. We finally made it to this place where we’re kind to each other, and we’re supportive of each other, and we’re making it work, co-parenting, in the personal lives and the professional lives. She also thinks about her kid. They have a kid who, if they try it again, they’re running him through this whole thing all over again, and I think that’s a big piece of why she’s like, we can’t do this. So I think even though it’s in J.D.’s fantasy, the writers wanted to show that that is Elliot’s take, so that then J.D. can be respectful of that, and his love for her supersedes his own wish to try it again.”

The vast majority of the fantasy sequence was shot in one day, chronologically, Chalke revealed.

“We actually got to shoot the whole dinner table scene over the first half the day, and then by the water for the second half of the day, which is really nice to get to film in order and all in one day,” she said. “As you know, with filming schedules that rarely happens, so that was a great way to get to do it.”

Filming the kiss scene in public with dozens of bystanders armed with cell phone watching proved a challenge but, luckily, no one ruined the surprise.

“We were shooting on the water in a very public setting, and we really didn’t want that moment to get spoiled,” Chalke said. “There were so many people, everybody with their camera phones, and we were like, ‘No!’ We shot the whole scene walking, and then once we stood, and we were just doing the overs to get that kiss scene, the grips put up giant flags to block it. There was water on one side of us, and then the street was on the other side. But with these giant flags, we only had enough to cover most of it. We could still see there was like four people filming. Once we did the kiss, we turned around and Zach just looked at them and he was like, ‘Please, please don’t spoil it.’ And nobody did.”

For fans who may have been disappointed to realize that J.D. and Elliot’s romantic reconciliation wasn’t real, there was that look at the end of the episode to hang onto. While J.D. was leaving the hospital at the end of the day, he glanced at Elliot who looked back at him.

Deadline asked Chalke how she interpreted it. Was this a precursor to what might come for the two of them or a final closure?

“I think it opens the door as opposed to closes it because we just understand so much more of how J.D. feels, we understand so much more of where his head is at and the fact that this is actually what he would love to try, but his love for Elliot is going to stop him from trying it,” she said.

While it was a fleeting moment in the episode, a lot of thought went into the scene.

“We actually shot a few different versions of my look to him because they shot it in slow motion, and we talked a lot about it of how to play that, if Elliot’s just doing her chart and it’s just business as usual, ‘Yep yep, bye, night,’ and has no idea, and then we had a couple more where they linger on the look a little bit longer.”

The deliberate thought process extended to the entire episode.

“It was a fun episode to do for that reason because there were so many conversations about where both of their heads were at, about what would come next, about how to not let the audience understand that it was a mislead. So there’s all these detailed conversations right down to Elliot’s wardrobe when she comes into the restaurant, what could she wear that’s in J.D.’s fantasy, but that also wouldn’t tip that Elliot understood why he was asking her to dinner. It was my favorite episode to shoot of the season for that reason, because there’s just so many fun things to dig into and to think about and to try and figure out how to come off successfully with the mislead, and also just have it be powerful for the audience.”

As for what the look means and whether there is a chance for J.D. and Elliot’s Episode 207 fantasy to become a reality, Chalke left the door open.

“Are we going to see more of that? I wish I could tell. I can’t because I don’t want to spoil anything. You have to watch to find out,” she said. “I hope we get to do more seasons so that we can really find out and really explore that more. Would be really cool.”

J.D.’s new love interest Charlie, played by Rachel Bilson, was introduced in the Season 1 finale. By the Season 2 premiere, the two were already an item, with J.D. happily flaunting his new relationship. Elliot got back in the dating game as marine biologist Sean (Scott Foley) reappeared life after her short-lived romance with the organ donor pilot fizzled. But her latest chapter with Sean didn’t stick either. By Episode 5, Charlie and Sean found themselves taking back seat to J.D. and Elliot’s commitment to their jobs and their patients and soon found a way to each other. Episode 5 ended with Charlie and Sean making out, rendering J.D. and Elliot single again.

Why did these relationships end so quickly? Were Charlie and Sean pushed aside so J.D. and Elliot are available to rekindle their own romance?

“I think part of that was also how many episodes that they could both do,” Chalke said about Bilson and Foley. “We really wanted to tell that story, I love the idea of when Sean says, you’re dating this mistress, the hospital as well and to show what that actually is really like, that J.D. and Elliot both have the best of intentions but these medical emergencies come up and they have to show up for them and then the two of them, Rachel and Scott’s characters, are left hanging out all the time.”

Chalke reminisced about Bilson and Foley’s short stints, wishing that they could be series regulars on the medical comedy.

“You’re right, it is a bit of a compressed way to tell the story but I think that they both brought so much to the show,” she said. “We all would have had them there forever, we were all like, they should be regulars. They’re so funny, they’re so much fun. We had the best time with them, and I love what they bring out in the other characters. Like, the writers were, how do we bring Elliot’s neuroses back from the OG days, and Sean’s character is the perfect way to make her flustered and off-balance because she has such a crush on him. I love Judy [Reyes]’s line where she says, “Oh, this is how we see that Elliot’s upward in her feelings again because she’s hitting her head and dropping the purse and doing all these things because she really likes him.”

Episode 207 finally introduced J.D. and Elliot’s talked about but not seen in the revival son Ollie, played by child actor Kellan Tetlow (This Is Us, Tracker).

The scene, which is tied to J.D. and Elliot’s fantasy date, had the two parents sit Ollie own to discuss relationships after finding out that he had a crush on a girl. (Turns out uncle Turk and aunt Carla had already given him the talk.)

“Overall, I think J.D. and Elliot have really put their kid first, I think they’re actually really great co-parents,” Chalke said. “They both do work, and their jobs are very important. They want to be really good doctors, and they really want to mentor these new kids [interns]. But I think the piece that we really want to get across is their kid has really come first.”

There was some confusion over how many children J.D. and Elliot have. Ahead of the revival’s premiere, Braff indicated to Deadline that they have two, Ollie and an older boy with whom Elliot was pregnant in Season 9 of the original series. That was later clarified, with the series’ writers opting for one child, Ollie, who was born years after the end of the original series. (Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence has said publicly that the revival is ignoring the existence of Season 9, which was a reboot.)

Chalke praised Tetlow, who is expected to appear in more episodes.

“J.D. and Elliot are great co-parents together, and then we’re super lucky to have cast a kid who’s fantastic,” she said. “He comes onto set, and he’s the sweetest kid. Scrubs is an environment where there’s four writers at a time by the monitors in Video Village making changes and coming up, saying, ‘Okay, so Sarah’s going to say this, and then you’re going to say this, and let’s try that. And here’s a new joke.” He is a young kid, and he rolls with all of it. That’s exciting because it makes us feel like we can really explore that more.”

Scrubs is known for its elaborate fantasy sequences. The one in Episode 207 of the revival was among the more challenging to pull off, with Chalke calling the technical aspects of the episode “super complex.”

She spoke about how the scenes with J.D. (Braff) joining his dementia-stricken patient on the ceiling and him pulling away from the fantasy into the real world came to life.

“The technical piece of this episode was incredible,” she said. “They built a full room upside down with a bed up on the top, and they had Zach in a harness, walking up the wall for the scene where we’re pulling away. They had this really cool set built, where it’s this long kind of tunnel that was actually built for this shot. The light sconces are on the sides, and if you watch, they’ve continued the light bars along the walls to make it look like it’s being stretched. Roger Fires, our [production designer], is incredibly talented, he was up all night thinking about it, and then 12 hours before we shot that, he’s like, ‘No, no, we need to build this platform because it needs to be on wheels, and Zach needs to be able to be standing on it so he can actually be on it while it’s getting pulled back.’ One of the coolest parts about working on this show is every department cares so much. You’ll get a script, and often they won’t have a lot of time to build it, and it’s everybody coming together, going, ‘Okay, how we problem solve and make this happen?'”

#3285. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

Here's what you get for the shockingly cheap price

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Over the past year, I’ve tested a handful of “affordable” EVs — which are, in a relative sense, priced lower than the national average of around $50,000. Depending on who you talk to, options below $40,000 look genuinely attractive, and anything under that threshold almost feels too good to be true.

Yet, that’s exactly where the Slate Truck lands with its $24,950 starting price. For an all-electric pickup, I have to admit I’m impressed by the genuine real-world capability it delivers on paper: a rear-mounted motor pushing 181 horsepower and 195 lb-ft of torque, a 65 kWh battery pack, 1,500 pounds of payload capacity, NACS DC fast-charging compatibility, and an estimated 205 miles of range.

While those specs might look modest next to six-figure behemoths like the Rivian R1T, Chevrolet Silverado EV, and GMC Sierra EV, you can't ignore just how accessible that price point is. But after getting up close with the Slate Truck in person, a few details caught me completely off guard. Here’s what stood out the most.

Prior to seeing the Slate Truck in person, I already knew it was scaling things back with crank windows and manual seats. Even in 2026, I still come across a handful of cars with manual seats — though that’s usually reserved strictly for the passenger side, and it's rarer still to find both seats manual.

So while manual adjustment wasn’t a shock, I was taken aback to find that the side mirrors are entirely manual, too. I can live with crank windows and mechanical seat levers, but manual side mirrors? That’s a tougher pill to swallow, simply because it’s been ages since I’ve had to adjust a mirror by hand.

The Slate Truck I saw featured a limited-edition wrap created in collaboration with Smarties. Yes, the candy rolls you probably remember from childhood.

Even though the "Blank Slate" base model rolls off the assembly line with a generic gray exterior, Slate sets itself apart by offering bold, fun vinyl wraps right out of the gate. It’s an ingenious way to make the truck feel uniquely yours, especially with options to match your personal style.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I’m just curious to see how well these wraps hold up after enduring a few harsh Northeast winters.

Compact pickups are already at a disadvantage due to their smaller footprint, and in a two-seater like the Slate Truck, cabin space is especially tight. Since the seats sit flush against the barrier separating the cabin from the flatbed, there’s practically no leeway to recline them for a more relaxed driving position.

That might not be an issue if the Slate Truck is strictly kept to quick local errands, but plenty of drivers will want to take it on longer road trips. Fighting driver fatigue starts with comfortable ergonomics, so the lack of recline here makes long stretches behind the wheel tough to manage.

I’ve seen deeper, longer beds on full-size pickups, but the Slate Truck’s usable cargo space rivals compact pickups I’ve tested, like the Hyundai Santa Cruz.

Personally, I think the bed is the perfect size for everyday needs — more than spacious enough for weekly Costco runs, while still handling the occasional large piece of furniture without breaking a sweat.

For many drivers, maneuvering into a tight parking spot is an everyday source of stress. Given the Slate Truck’s aggressive cost-cutting measures, I worried that a backup camera might have been left out — but thankfully, it wasn't.

As federal regulations mandate rear-visibility systems on all new vehicles, Slate included one by mounting an integrated camera right near the tailgate latch, taking the guesswork and anxiety out of parallel parking.

Even knowing the Slate Truck favors a minimalist approach, stepping inside the cabin to find it so stripped-back is an eye-opener. It’s a refreshingly clutter-free dashboard: simple mechanical climate knobs and an integrated phone mount anchor the center dash, while slim air vents span nearly the full width of the interior.

Behind the steering wheel sits a compact digital instrument cluster displaying only essential driving telemetry. It’s an minimalist setup that cuts out distractions and keeps your focus squarely on the road.

The biggest challenge the Slate Truck faces is convincing buyers the company will actually be around for the life of the vehicle. Given its ultra-aggressive pricing, I’m genuinely surprised the EV maker is offering such a generous 10-year, 110,000-mile battery and powertrain warranty.

For a startup automaker, including this coverage at no extra charge gives budget-conscious drivers real peace of mind that a cheap entry price won’t turn into a financial money pit down the road.

#3283. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3282. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

#3281. Charles Porter Dies: ‘Finding Faith’ Producer & Actor Was 47

Charles F. Porter, the actor and producer known for backing the 2025 film Finding Faith and playing the titular NASCAR phenom in ESPN’s Wendell Scott: A Race Story, died on Monday after a long battle with cancer. His passing was announced by his wife, Candice Tab-Porter. He was 47.

Porter was a multihyphenate in more ways than one. Born in the U.K., he went to college at Duke, where he played defensive end on the school’s football team. After a back injury derailed his NFL hopes, Porter dropped 65 pounds and became an actor.

In the early 2000s, he made appearances on The Parkers, Close to Home, Without a Trace, Bones and House.

In 2011, he landed the lead in Wendell Scott: A Race Story. The ESPN TV movie was based on the story of Wendell Scott, who in 1963 became the first and only African-American to ever win a NASCAR Cup race. Porter was the lead. Watch on Deadline

He was also the lead and a producer on Image Entertainment’s 2006 horror thriller Nailed. Additionally, he had a small part in STX’s Jennifer Garner vehicle Peppermint.

Last year, Porter produced Lifetime’s Finding Faith starring Paula Patton, Stephen Bishop, Keith David and Nadine Velazquez. He also had a small part in the film as a bartender.

Porter is survived by his wife, Candice, and two daughters, Juliette and Layla.

Tackling baked-on oven grease is rarely anyone’s favorite chore, but the shortcuts you take to get the job done could be silently wrecking your cooker.

According to one appliance expert, several well-meaning cleaning methods can damage your appliance’s surface and reduce its performance.

While you might feel confident with how to clean your oven, Ecem Uslubaş, senior product manager for cooking at Hotpoint, says, “a lot of common habits are based on what’s always been done rather than what works for each surface.”

And she adds, “Getting it wrong doesn’t always cause obvious damage straight away, but it can impact the performance of your appliance without regular care.”

So, before you slip on your household gloves and give your oven a deep clean, consider these six common oven-cleaning mistakes — and the safer routines you should adopt instead.

Reaching for the same abrasive scourer for the cooktop, the oven interior and the exterior trim is one of the most common habits.

“Enamel, glass and stainless steel all respond differently to abrasive materials," explains Uslubaş. “A sponge tough enough for baked-on food can leave fine scratches on glass or dull the finish on stainless steel over time.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Instead of using the same cleaning sponge for all surfaces, she suggests keeping a softer cloth aside for delicate surfaces and reserving anything abrasive for tougher, more durable areas, as it will help protect each surface for longer.

Wiping a spill away once the cooker has cooled is far easier than dealing with it after several more cooking cycles.

“Each time a spill gets reheated, it bonds more firmly to the surface,” says Uslubaş. “What would have taken a quick wipe on day one can end up needing a specialist product and more effort a few weeks later.”

Even though it can seem easy to close the oven door and pretend the mess doesn’t exist, it will only prolong and worsen the cleanup. Instead of a simple wipe-down, your oven will need a deep clean if spills are left to solidify and become baked-in.

Aiming a spray bottle straight at the controls can allow liquid to seep behind buttons or dials, which may affect how they function. However, there’s a simple way to change this habit, protecting your appliance while still getting it clean.

“It’s worth applying the product to a cloth first, rather than spraying it directly onto the panel,” advises Uslubaş.

Shelves, trays and other removable parts vary between cooker models, and not all of them are suited to a dishwasher cycle.

It's also worth being aware that some finishes can be affected by the heat or the detergents used in a dishwasher, which makes them unsuitable, while some parts may only be suitable for cleaning on the top rack.

Uslubaş says, "Make sure you check the appliance instructions before removing or washing any parts of your appliance. It’s also worth checking before using any specialist cleaning product too.”

Lining the bottom of the oven with foil might seem like a simple way to catch spills, but it can interfere with airflow and heat distribution. Although it's easier to remove and replace soiled foil, it has a negative impact on the performance of your oven.

"Ovens are designed with specific airflow in mind, and foil can disrupt that, leading to uneven cooking results," explains Uslubaş.

As an alternative she suggests using removable trays or liners designed for the purpose, as they are a safer way to catch drips without affecting performance.

This Whirlpool electric range features two ovens and has a combined capacity of 6.7 cubic feet, with plenty of space to cook multiple foods at different temperatures. Plus, with 5 burners and Aqua-Lift self-cleaning technology, it's hard to beat.

The door seal is one of the most frequently missed areas during a routine clean, despite playing an important role in how efficiently the oven heats. I have to admit, that I also neglect cleaning my washing machine and dishwasher seal, just the same.

"Seals can gather grease and food debris just like any other part of the oven, and a damaged or dirty seal can let heat escape," says Uslubaş. “Wiping around the seal and door edges as part of a regular clean helps maintain both hygiene and cooking performance.”

Regularly cleaning the seal also lets you check for wear, such as cracks that can reduce the seal’s efficiency.

Cleaning an oven can be a real drag, especially after you've cooked a roast, as the entire appliance can be covered in grease. But, it can be made easier by cleaning it out once it's cooled down, rather than leaving until it's cooked a few more dinners. However, if you are in the market for one of the best ovens, Uslubaş says it’s worth looking for an appliance that helps clean itself, and suggests buying one with the following features:Pyrolytic cleaningThe oven heats up to an extreme temperature and carbonizes and incinerates grease, baked-on food and residue to a fine ash.

Steam cleaningRather than heating to extreme temperatures, a steam cleaning function involves pouring a small amount of water onto the oven floor and heating it to around 200-400°F. The steam created helps loosen any residue, which can then be wiped away with a cloth.

Catalytic linersThe oven’s interior walls are lined with a porous enamel embedded with an oxidation catalyst. The liner continuously absorbs grease and food splatters while you’re baking at normal temperatures.

#3276. Harold Greene Dies: Longtime L.A. News Anchor Was 82

Harold Greene, the likeable longtime news anchor for many of L.A.’s local news stations, died last night. His passing was announced by family. Greene was 82.

At various junctures in his career, Greene worked for ABC7 Eyewitness News, KCAL 9 News and CBS 2 News. Greene also worked in San Diego for a period, and legend has long had it that his on-air look at the time (including an impressive mustache) inspired elements of the Ron Burgundy character in Anchorman. Will Ferrell has denied this, however.

Greene got his first job in L.A. as a reporter and producer for KABC. Shortly thereafter, he left for the San Diego affiliate, KCST-TV (now KNSD). He then jumped to the NBC affiliate at the time, KGTV, to co-anchor the news.

In 1978, he co-anchored the news in L.A. with Eyewitness News legend Jerry Dunphy. He became ABC7’s weekend anchor with Joanne Ishimine in 1982 before taking over the anchor chair for the 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. weeknight editions of Eyewitness News after Dunphy left. He later moved to the 5 p.m. and 11 p.m. slots. At ABC, Greene also hosted locally produced light-news programs such as Hollywood Close-Up and A.M. Los Angeles.

In 2001, he moved to CBS 2 and was part of a formidable on-air lineup that included L.A. TV News stalwarts Ann Martin and sportscaster Jim Hill. Later, Laura Diaz and weatherman Johnny Mountain joined the crew, reuniting members of KABC’s Eyewitness News team from the 1980s and early 1990s. Greene and Martin were laid off by KCBS/KCAL in 2008.

Greene received 10 Golden Mike awards, the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism Award, two Emmys, three Edward R. Murrow Awards and twelve L.A. Press Club Awards.

His daughter Courtney announced the news, writing that her father had “signed off for the last time” on Tuesday. She added that she and her mother were with Greene when he passed.

‘We have a feeling he’s already settling into the great newsroom in the sky, no doubt with a few suggestions on how things should be run.”

A memorial is being planned for after the holidays.

Here’s how to tweak your device to help you reach your goals

If one of your health goals is to lose weight, wearing a fitness tracker, including one of the best Apple Watches, is a great place to start. To lose weight and keep it off, you’ll need to ensure you’re burning more calories than you consume — otherwise known as a calorie deficit.

One of the easiest ways to see how many calories you’re burning is to wear a fitness tracker. Yet, if you’ve got an Apple Watch on your wrist, how you set up your watch can make all the difference. Read on to find out more.

As a reminder, if you’re looking for personalized advice when it comes to weight loss, it’s always a good idea to talk to your physician.

Whether you choose the Apple Watch SE 3, the Apple Watch Series 12, or invest in the Apple Watch Ultra 4, there are a few ways to ensure your watch gives you the most accurate health data. Here are three top tips:

Let’s caveat something here: no smartwatch or sports watch on the market will be 100% accurate when it comes to estimating how many calories you’ve actually burned. They largely rely on algorithms, and to really get an idea of your true energy expenditure every day, you’d need to be wired up in a lab.

That said, your Apple Watch will estimate your calorie expenditure using your heart rate data, as well as your personal metrics, plus data from the movement sensors and GPS. How accurately your watch records all of this data depends on how well it fits.

Your Apple Watch should be snug, not tight, with the heart rate sensor sitting flush against your wrist. The watch should sit above your wrist bone, and it shouldn’t be loose enough to rotate as you move.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Remember those personal metrics I just mentioned that form part of the calorie expenditure algorithm on your Apple Watch? It’s important to make sure these are accurate, especially as you start losing weight, because they can make a big difference.

It’s also important to ensure that your Apple Watch is calibrated, as this makes the data more accurate. Firstly, head to Location Services on your iPhone, click System Services, then Motion Calibration and Distance and make sure it’s turned on. Next, go for a 20-minute walk in a flat area where you can see clear blue skies (heavily wooded areas or skyscrapers can affect GPS) at your natural pace wearing the Apple Watch, as this will make sure it’s calibrated to your stride.

Finally, another important step when it comes to getting the most accurate idea of your calorie expenditure is to choose the right workout mode on your Apple Watch. Each workout type will use a specialized algorithm tailored to the expected movement pattern.

For example, I’d often use Functional Strength Training mode during my HIIT workouts in the gym. When I switched to using High-Intensity Interval Training, my average calorie burn was higher. This is because the Apple Watch is weighing the elevated heart rate that comes with a HIIT session with short periods of rest more heavily than it would in strength training mode.

Of course, even when your watch is set up perfectly, it’s important to reiterate again that no wearable will be perfect when it comes to estimating your overall calorie expenditure. The best way to lose weight is to eat a balanced, healthy diet, prioritize movement, and focus on your overall health.

#3273. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3272. How Joe Miñoso Exits ‘Chicago Fire’ As Cruz In Season 15

SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points for NBC‘s Chicago Fire‘s Season 15 Episode 5 titled “Three Hundred.”

It’s the end of an era on NBC’s Chicago Fire, as we say goodbye to Joe Miñoso, who has played Firefighter Josef “Joe” Cruz since Season 1. And what better way to send him off than on the show’s 300th episode titled “Three Hundred.” Check out Deadline’s interview with Miñoso, where he talks about saying goodbye after close to 15 years.

It never gets any easier saying goodbye to actors who leave the series, especially those who have been on the show since Day 1 like Miñoso. But it certainly helps when we see them get their happily ever after, which was the case for Joe, who’s been having a rough go at things since the Season 15 premiere when he suffered a spine injury. Through hardships, the character learns a lot about himself and what he really wants out of life. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News 'Worth' Detective Drama From Mike Diliberti, Jake Coburn & Jack Carr In Development At NBC Late Night TV 'SNL' Pays Tribute To Patrick Stewart With Clip From His 1994 Episode

The episode opens with Joe getting physical therapy, showing off how far he has advanced in re-learning how to walk. You can feel how dedicated he is to improving his health and getting back to life by how he focuses on breaking his own record of steps.

Later, Joe shows up at 51 and surprises his team with a visit. He reunites with Capp (Randy Flagler), Tony (Anthony Ferraris), and Severide (Taylor Kinney), whom he shares a medical update with. With a big smile on his face, Joe rises from his wheelchair before them and jokes, “My legs finally got the memo.”

He tells the guys that Dr. Archer (Steven Webber from Chicago Med) let him know about some specialized recovery centers that help first responders get back to their jobs. He’s hopeful that within a few months, he will be cleared to get back to life as he once knew it. Seconds later, the fire truck arrives at the station, and Mouch (Christian Stolte) yells out loud, “Joe Cruz!” The rest of the team excitedly celebrates the visit before Severide beckons him to his office.

Battalion Chief Tomlin, played by Doug Savant of Melrose Place and Desperate Housewives fame, invites himself into Severide’s office first to tell him that they need to begin their search for Joe’s replacement. Tomlin gives Severide one week to submit the name of a qualified candidate before headquarters makes the choice for him.

Joe heads home where his wife, Chloe Cruz (Kristen Gutoskie), is busy around the house trying to get things in order while heavily pregnant with twins. She expresses her stress and frustration about all of the responsibilities that have fallen on her since the accident and that she desperately needs help. During the discussion, Chloe starts going into labor and her water breaks. Joe was certain they still had time before the babies would make their grand appearance, as expected, four weeks later, but it soon becomes very real that they’re running out of time.

Joe and their two sons rush Chloe to Gaffney Chicago Medical Center, where she gives birth to two little girls, whom they name Sofia and Elena. Dr. Archer stops by to congratulate the Cruz family and welcome Joe to the #girldad club. Archer reveals he had a chat with his physical therapist, who said his progress was remarkable and that he would hopefully be ready to return to work. The disappointed reaction from Chloe and the kids was expected, but Joe is finally realizing he needs to think about what his family needs now the most.

Joe reconnects with Severide and lets him know, with tears in his eyes, that he’s decided to not come back to 51. He and the family will be moving to Minneapolis to be near Chloe’s mom, who is excited to help them out with the newborns, leaving Joe time to join a program in the Minnesota city. Severide is stunned to hear his decision; after 12 years of riding together, nothing will ever be the same.

The episode ends with Joe paying a visit to Otis’ (Yuriy Sardarov) memorial, which he’s kept an eye on since his death in the Season 8 premiere in 2019. With a promise that Capp and Tony will keep the marble well looked after, Joe says, “I’ll be with you always, brother.”

Severide shows up from behind to congratulate his friend with a cigar in hand, for the man of the hour. The final beats of the episode show Joe surrounded by the devoted and beloved group of men and women he has worked with for more than a decade for a final photo. Right smack in the middle, Joe smiles for the photo, knowing that his contributions to the team will never be forgotten.

#3271. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3270. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s revamped StandBy to other iPhones

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in December. To learn more about StandBy and how to customize its different faces, follow this link.

There’s plenty to watch across the major streaming services this week, but some movies and shows won’t be sticking around for much longer. From Netflix and Prime Video to Peacock and Tubi, several titles are preparing to leave their respective platforms over the next few days.

That means it’s time to check your watchlist and see if there’s anything you’ve been putting off. I’ve rounded up 40 movies and shows worth catching before they disappear, including a few hidden gems, familiar favorites and titles you might have missed the first time around.

Whether you’re after a gripping horror flick, a compelling crime film, or something a little more romantic, there’s plenty to choose from. So, if any of these have been sitting on your watchlist, now might be the time to watch before they’re gone.

What it's about: In this horror movie, a masked serial killer known as the Heart Eyes Killer has spent years targeting couples on Valentine's Day. When advertising colleagues Ally (Olivia Holt) and Jay (Mason Gooding) are mistaken for a loved-up pair, they find themselves in the killer's crosshairs. Forced to spend the most romantic night of the year fighting for their lives, the unlikely duo must put their differences aside to survive.

Why you should watch it: “Heart Eyes” is a bloody good time if you enjoy your horror with a healthy dose of comedy. Olivia Holt and Mason Gooding have great chemistry, while the movie's masked killer delivers some genuinely nasty surprises along the way. I also love how it plays around with familiar slasher tropes, including gruesome kills and creepy moments with plenty of laughs. It's a fun, entertaining watch that doesn't take itself too seriously.

Watch "Heart Eyes" on Netflix until Nov. 8

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What it's about: After a series of brutal murders in a small New Mexico town, two FBI agents arrive to investigate and question three survivors: a troubled police officer, a drug-addicted young woman and an eight-year-old girl. Using surveillance footage and witness interviews, they attempt to piece together what happened during a violent roadside rampage. However, the conflicting accounts reveal that not everyone is telling the truth, and the real story is far more disturbing than it first appears.

Why you should watch it: Jennifer Lynch’s “Surveillance” is a seriously twisted thriller that keeps you guessing right up to its brutal finale. Bill Pullman and Julia Ormond deliver particularly strong performances, while the unsettling atmosphere and unpredictable storytelling make it difficult to know where things are heading. The nonlinear structure slowly pieces together the mystery. It's a nasty, gripping watch that should appeal to anyone who enjoys thrillers with a few surprises up their sleeve.

Watch "Surveillance" on Prime Video until Nov. 10

What it's about: Based on Colleen Hoover's bestselling novel, this romantic drama follows Kenna (Maika Monroe), who returns to her Wyoming hometown seven years after a tragic accident landed her in prison. Hoping to reconnect with her young daughter, Diem, she faces rejection from the grandparents raising her. However, Kenna finds an unexpected ally in Ledger (Tyriq Withers), a local bar owner with connections to her daughter's family.

Why you should watch it: “Reminders of Him” is a heartfelt romantic drama that should appeal to anyone who enjoys an emotional love story. Maika Monroe delivers a strong lead performance, bringing plenty of feeling to a story about grief, forgiveness and getting a second chance at happiness. The movie has all the ingredients fans have come to expect from Hoover's work, including complicated relationships and some genuinely moving moments. Keep the tissues handy for this one!

#3268. Joe Miñoso Talks Cruz’s Exit From ‘Chicago Fire,’ Storylines That Almost Happened & Plans To Direct

SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points from tonight’s episode of NBC‘s Chicago Fire.

NBC’s Chicago Fire celebrated its landmark 300th episode tonight, and it was bittersweet. While there was a lot to celebrate, it also marked Day 1’er Joe Miñoso’s final episode in the firefighter drama after 14+ years portraying the beloved Joe Cruz. And even though the character may have moved on to Minnesota with his family, Miñoso has been shadowing directors on set with the goal of directing an upcoming yet-to-be-determined episode.

“It was ultimately an appropriately timed choice. I think that both the team and I knew it in one way or the other. And when the time came, it just kind of felt like, yeah. You know, 300 is such a good number. It is such a gift to say that I did five of these episodes, let alone 300-plus across the three shows. It was a bittersweet moment,” Miñoso told Deadline earlier this week. Related Stories News 'Worth' Detective Drama From Mike Diliberti, Jake Coburn & Jack Carr In Development At NBC Late Night TV 'SNL' Pays Tribute To Patrick Stewart With Clip From His 1994 Episode

“An hour after I found out, I heard there was an opportunity to direct if I wanted it. So it was very whiplashy. It was such an insane back-and-forth, but at the same time, it just felt very right. I’m excited to grow into the next chapter. I’ve been directing and producing for a while, some of my own stuff. So it just felt like a natural evolution,” he added. Watch on Deadline

Learn more about Cruz’s fate in Deadline’s recap of Episode 5, aptly titled “Three Hundred.” Below, read more about our chat with Miñoso.

DEADLINE: Cruz is usually the fun guy, so it was tough to watch him struggle this season. What was it like playing a different side of this character?

JOE MIÑOSO: It was a welcome challenge. I appreciate everything that these writers have thrown at me over the course of the last 14 and a half seasons. It has always been a surprise and a joy. Everything has its different difficulty level. I think back to the longest one-er we’ve done on this show, which involved Chloe [Kristen Gutoskie] in a crash and me kind of running through this giant wreckage. That was, in its own way, a tremendous experience as a performer, especially working in film. You know the elevator episode with David Eigenberg, which was us in an elevator. We filmed 30 pages a day, which is unheard of. It was like being in a play. There are so many things to be proud of, and so many moments that I feel like I’ve learned so much and I’ve grown so much, and that’s all due to the show.

DEADLINE: There was a powerful scene at the end of this episode where Cruz and Severide (Taylor Kinney) have a 1:1 conversation. What can you share about shooting those scenes with him?

MIÑOSO: It will forever be my favorite scene that I’ve ever had with him. I don’t think we’ve really had the opportunity to explore these two men on equal footing in a really intimate way ever. In general, Severide is a man of few words. He’s a stoic human being who doesn’t really share much of what he’s going through. We’ve seen Kidd (Miranda Rae Mayo) over the years chip away at that wall. But he was so vulnerable in that scene. So many of the things we were saying could have very easily been Joe and Taylor talking in terms of our history together on the show. And it was, and will forever remain. I’m really proud that we had the conversation in general, and we got to see a different dynamic between the two.

DEADLINE: Joe’s storyline this season felt very much like, if something major didn’t stop him in his tracks, he wouldn’t have quit 51. Do you agree that sometimes life has to make us uncomfortable before we realize that it’s time to move on?

MIÑOSO: Yeah, I agree with you. The decision was made for him when he saw that the family had reached a new level and that he was needed in a different way. What’s so brilliant about that is that the first real storyline we see for Cruz is him possibly sacrificing his entire life and livelihood for the sake of his brother by leaving a gang member to burn in a building. Technically, he gives up and decides to leave the fire department because he thinks he can’t get over his own guilt over what he’s done. It takes one of his brothers, Mouch [Christian Stolte], to convince him otherwise. So to go from that to a man who is willing to give up his identity after all these years, ultimately, for the sake of his family, feels like we’re kind of at the beginning. He’s just grown into a different position.

DEADLINE: As a fan, things were pretty touch and go. We were scared they would kill off Cruz.

MIÑOSO: That was discussed. That was one of the options that was thrown out there. I won’t say by who, but yeah, that was pitched. But to [showrunner] Victor [Teran’s] and the writers’ credit, they decided that they’d rather go through this more emotional arc. I was honored by that because it was a big responsibility. It’s a large weight to carry, and I’m so glad they trusted me.

DEADLINE: That final moment when Cruz visits Otis’ [Yuri Sardarov] memorial was very emotional for me as a viewer. What did that scene mean to you?

MIÑOSO: That scene was actually my suggestion. There’s so much for the writers to think about when they’re writing for 9k characters and 20 million plot points to deal with. A lot can go under the radar. I just felt like we really needed to put a period on that relationship. They’re so intertwined, and he has still been such an integral part of Cruz’s life. It’s so obvious that Cruz is cleaning this memorial all the time. Now he’s passing those duties on.

The fact that the last words that Yuri says on the show are “I will be there with you always, brother,” and the opportunity to reflect on that felt like something that would not only honor the character but also the fans that have been with us for so long. I fell in love with those two as a team. That scene was hard to film. As I told the director, I want this to feel hopeful. I want this to be about the love of these two brothers, and I don’t want it to be sad. I don’t know that I’m going to be able to get a take without crying, because it was just so loaded. Yuri and I are still remarkable friends. We’re talking now more than ever because we’re in the middle of trying to get this rewatch podcast off the ground.

MIÑOSO: It’s brand new. We’re really just in the beginning phases of seeing if we can make something work. We just want to be able to celebrate the show and the friendship that we’ve built for the world.

DEADLINE: Did you tell Yuri about Otis being represented in your final episode?

MIÑOSO: Yes, I told him that there would be a moment. We were actually hoping that we could figure out how he could come back. But it felt right. I think this gives you the opportunity to miss Otis that much more. There was a moment where I maybe threw something out like [Otis] is the guy that gets Cruz out of the burning building. We had explored something like that earlier last year during our Halloween episode, where Cruz comes across this random old dude who is never seen again, and we allude to the fact that he was a ghost.

DEADLINE: Would you like to share any parting words for the fans?

MIÑOSO: Thank you forever. I recognize that the success of any character or any show is always driven by the people who watch it. I so appreciate you all giving me the opportunity to live in this guy’s skin for so many years. It doesn’t go unnoticed by me how important your support for the character has been, and I’m forever grateful to all of you for letting me enjoy this for as long as I have.

Now, with Xcode 27.3, Apple is expanding the list of supported AI coding tools once again, this time adding GitHub Copilot.

As with the other agentic integrations, this is particularly good news for developers whose companies have standardized on GitHub Copilot, as they can now use their company’s preferred AI coding tool directly within Xcode.

Xcode 27.3 beta includes Swift 6.4 and SDKs for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, tvOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.
