#3208. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3207. Barcelona’s Kabilio raises €10M to bring AI agents to accounting firms

Picus Capital and Visionaries led the round as the startup nears 500 client firms, up from 100 a year ago.

Kabilio co-founders and co-CEOs Jose Ojeda and Álex Valls

Barcelona startup Kabilio, which wants AI to take the receipt-chasing out of accounting, has raised €10M in a round led by Picus Capital and Visionaries. CDTI, Spain’s public agency for technology and innovation, also took part.

Both lead investors also backed the company’s €4m pre-seed round a year ago, and the new money brings its total funding to €14m. Since then, Kabilio has grown from about 100 accounting firms to nearly 500, and its team to 80 people.

Those firms do a job most small businesses would rather not. Across Spain and much of Europe, small companies pass their books and taxes to an outside firm. There, much of the work still means sorting invoices and matching payments by hand.

Kabilio started there. Its software reads invoices, suggests how to book them, matches bank transactions and flags anything odd, while the accountant reviews and signs off. Kabilio says this saves accountants about 60% of their bookkeeping and reconciliation time.

“Nobody becomes an accountant to chase receipts, and nobody starts a business to do paperwork,” said Jose Ojeda, Kabilio’s co-founder and co-CEO.

The new capital pays for the next step: an AI agent that firms can hand whole tasks to, much as they would a new hire. It will gather invoices and bank statements from inboxes, reconcile accounts, check entries and chase gaps, even messaging clients by email or WhatsApp.

The agent enters beta this month, and several firms are already testing it. Accountants keep the reins, giving it instructions in plain language and deciding, client by client, how much it may do on its own.

Kabilio is also bringing the firms’ clients onto the same platform. Kabilio Empresas, launched in September, lets small businesses invoice, link their bank accounts and watch their cash flow in the system their accountant uses. The company then sees new figures as they arrive instead of at tax time.

Later, the company plans to turn the agent towards those businesses too, sending invoices, nudging late payers and answering everyday tax questions for owners. Clients join only through their accountant, who sets the agent’s limits.

“An agent is only as good as the data it works on,” said Álex Valls, Kabilio’s other co-founder and co-CEO.

Kabilio is entering a busy field, as belgian startup Ravical raised a $17m seed round last week for its own AI platform for accounting firms, while Visa is piloting AI agents that pay supplier invoices.

#3205. Report: Apple reduces employees’ AI token allowances as Ternus moves to cut costs

Bloomberg reports that Apple has begun reducing employees’ daily AI spending limits, with some engineers seeing their allowances cut from $300 to $200, and further reductions planned across multiple teams. Here are the details.

Over the past year, tokenmaxxing, the practice of consuming as many AI tokens as possible, often as a measure of productivity, took over Silicon Valley, with companies such as Meta even introducing internal leaderboards, some unofficial, ranking employees by their AI token usage.

Tokenmaxxing emerged alongside improvements in AI agents’ coding capabilities, as tools such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor became increasingly popular among software developers.

Unsurprisingly, companies soon began to rein in token usage as the rising costs of AI tools raised questions about whether the productivity gains justified the expense. Just recently, Accenture reportedly reduced its centrally funded Claude allowance to just $29 per employee per month, requiring any additional spending to be covered by individual projects or teams.

And while there hadn’t been reports of disproportionate token usage from engineers and other employees at Apple, Bloomberg reported today that the company is also looking to rein in employees’ AI spending as part of CEO John Ternus’ broader cost-cutting efforts.

Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap for some engineers using AI models to $200 from $300, according to people with knowledge of the change. The company is now planning further cuts for some engineering teams, potentially reducing their daily allowances to as little as $100, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams, the people said. Employees who require higher allowances to perform their jobs will be able to seek exemptions from senior leadership.

It is not immediately clear which tools are affected by the new spending limits. However, Bloomberg reports that Apple employees have access to several AI services, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini. Some teams are also being encouraged to use cheaper AI models or models that run locally on their devices to reduce costs.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman had previously said that Apple was heavily reliant on Anthropic’s AI models for its internal operations, describing the company as essentially “running on Anthropic,” despite its partnership with Google to power Siri.

That came a few months after then-CEO Tim Cook encouraged employees to make greater use of AI in their daily work during an all-hands meeting, saying, “All of us are using AI in a significant way already, and we must use it as a company as well.”

$200-$300 per day is a pretty high amount. There are certainly people and tasks that can effectively put that many tokens to efficient use, but my guess is that most people bumping those limits could be more efficient in their use.

You’re going to always have that one person who complains about the budget but is out there making small code changes running Fable on max. These blanket token budgets typically seek to limit damage from those types while those that can make a case for why they need more budget typically get it.

Back to today’s report, Bloomberg says employee reactions to the new spending limits have been mixed. According to its sources, “few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances,” while others “see the reductions as a sign of broader cost cutting, adding to concerns about potential layoffs.”

Interestingly, the cuts come as Apple’s overall spending continues to rise. Earlier this week, Apple reported its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings, bringing its fiscal year to a close with R&D expenses up 32% to $45.8 billion, driven in part by higher infrastructure and AI costs.

Bloomberg notes that it remains unclear how much Apple will actually save through the new restrictions, particularly since some employees weren’t using their full allowances to begin with.

#3204. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3203. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3202. Apple disables Siri AI waitlist in iOS 27, with one exception

When Siri AI launched in iOS 27 earlier this fall, Apple used a waitlist to gate access. But a newly updated support document says the waitlist is no longer being used, except in “high demand” times.

If you haven’t yet enabled Siri AI on your iPhone, Apple recently made it quicker and easier to gain access.

That’s because, per updates to this support document, the company is now only using a waitlist for Siri AI in “high demand” times.

After giving instructions on how to enable Siri AI by tapping “Try Siri AI (Beta)” inside Settings, here’s what the document used to say compared to what it says now.

This will add you to a waitlist, and wait times can vary. Siri AI will begin to download automatically when your wait is complete.

Siri AI will begin to download automatically. During time of high demand, you might be added to a waitlist first, and wait times can vary.

It’s understandable that a waitlist was used initially upon iOS 27’s release. Apple needed to slowly grant access while gauging server performance. But now that we’re nearly two months into the iOS 27 rollout, it’s great that Apple is only deploying the waitlist occasionally as needed.

Have you enabled Siri AI on your iPhone? If not, what’s holding you back? Let us know in the comments.

#3200. Apple Photos keeps getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

iOS 27’s biggest highlight is Siri AI, but the update also packs new features for apps like Messages, Notes, Wallet, and more. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Photos app in iOS 27.

Apple Intelligence powers a trio of editing tools in iOS 27’s Photos app: Extend, Reframe, and a much-improved Clean Up feature.

Extend lets users “give their subjects more breathing room,” per Apple. For example, “they can straighten a crooked horizon without cropping out anything important, or adjust the aspect ratio, and Extend will fill in the missing pieces.”

Reframe lets you adjust the framing of your image spatially. Here’s how Apple describes it:

With Spatial Reframing, users can improve the composition of a photo after it’s been taken. Spatial Reframing builds on Apple’s deep understanding of spatial models thanks to Apple Vision Pro, so users can touch and drag a photo and preview in real time how the perspective shifts — as if they’d repositioned the camera in the original scene. Using powerful image models, Spatial Reframing will only generate new content where the perspective has been shifted, ensuring the reframed photo stays consistent with the original scene.

And the Clean Up feature that debuted in iOS 18 “gets a major upgrade,” Apple says, “so users can remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex.”

iCloud Shared Albums get their first major upgrades in years with iOS 27. The timing is likely no coincidence, with the feature perfect for Apple’s new HomeView product.

Here’s an overview of what’s new, per Apple:

iOS 27 adds two new collections to the Photos app, available under Utilities.

Captured by Me exclusively contains photos taken by you. So it will filter out screenshots, photos you’ve saved from others, and so on.

Identity Documents scans through your Photos library and surfaces images that contain important reference documents, like your driver’s license or passport.

Apple says iOS 27 also adds “Album organization improvements,” but it doesn’t mention specifics.

Another new organization tool in iOS 27 is that you can add keywords to photos. Captions are still available too, but if you scroll up on a photo, near the bottom you’ll find a new ‘Add Keywords’ option.

Another upgrade perfect for HomeView involves slideshow improvements.

Apple Photos has supported quick, easy slideshow creation for years. But if you wanted to customize the automatically generated slideshows, you were out of luck.

Now in iOS 27, slideshows offer new tools for customization. You can change the transition type, set a custom length for the full slideshow and for each photo, and more.

Another welcome addition is that Apple now lets you save any slideshow as a video with one tap.

iOS 27 doesn’t contain any big changes to the design of the Photos app, so if you were hoping to go back to the pre-iOS 18 era, you’ll be disappointed. But the update does offer a variety of exciting new features that make iOS 27 a big release for Apple Photos.

Which of iOS 27’s new Apple Photos features are your favorites? Let us know in the comments.

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Ryan got his start in journalism as an Editor at MacStories, where he worked for four years covering Apple news, writing app reviews, and more. For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad. As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

#3199. Intrepid Potash (IPI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Trio output climbed 19% as Moab harvest timing shifted.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Intrepid Potash, Inc. (IPI +1.72%) reported its third quarter results, highlighting a strategy focused on operational execution and capital discipline. Management reported increased Trio production and improved segment gross margins despite seasonal weakness and a strategic delay in the potash harvest season. The company stated that it is prioritizing organic growth through investments in its existing assets while returning capital to shareholders through share repurchases. Additionally, the company noted that selection for federal matching funding for a new sulfate of potash facility represents a potential expansion into specialty fertilizer markets.

Operator: Thank you for standing by. This is the conference moderator. Welcome to the Intrepid Potash Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] The conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to Ryan Schultz, Investor Relations Manager. Please go ahead.

Ryan Schultz: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us to discuss Intrepid's third quarter 2026 results. With me today are Kevin Crutchfield, our Chief Executive Officer; Zach Adams, our Vice President of Sales and Marketing; Rick Kim, our Vice President of Operations; and Jason Tremblay, our Chief Financial Officer. Before I turn the call over to Kevin, I want to remind everyone that today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about future business and financial expectations. The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 provides a safe harbor from civil litigation for such forward-looking statements.

Actual results may differ significantly from those projected in today's forward-looking statements due to various risks and uncertainties, including the risks described in our periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements. Further, this call will include the discussion of certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliation of these measures to the closest GAAP financial measure is included in our earnings press release and corresponding SEC filings, which are available at intrepidpotash.com. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kevin.

Kevin Crutchfield: Thank you, Ryan, and good morning, everyone. On last quarter's call, I discussed the 3 pillars of our own value creation strategy: execution, opportunity, and capital discipline. We made good progress on all 3 of these fronts during the third quarter. With respect to our execution, we increased production in Trio during the third quarter. This operating performance supports a 10,000 ton increase in our full year 2026 Trio production guidance and positions us to target annual production of more than 300,000 tons, a goal we didn't expect to achieve until sometime in 2027. We're acutely focused on the reliability and predictability of our operations, and we're pleased with the improving track record that we're establishing.

Rick will discuss the operating drivers behind this progress shortly. With respect to opportunity as the only U.S.-based producer of muriate of potash and 1 of only 2 global producers of langbeinite, the mineral we market as Trio, we see significant potential to unlock value through organic growth investment. In potash, our opportunity lies in our ability to increase production while moving down the cost curve through operational excellence. We expect to lower production costs, and combined with our transportation cost advantage in our core markets and the diversity of our offerings, we expect to drive profitable growth in our potash business. Trio's combination of low chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfate gives us a differentiated platform for growth.

We believe that potential growth in demand for sulfur nutrition could support this opportunity over time. Zach will discuss the market backdrop for the products in more detail shortly. We believe consistent execution, rigorous cost controls, and strategic organic growth investments can unlock the earnings potential of our existing assets, driving profitability and improved free cash flow conversion. While cyclical, the domestic market for agricultural nutrient is large, and third-party industry forecasts generally anticipate growth over the coming years. Importantly, as we've seen in recent years, the fertilizer market is highly sensitive to global geopolitical disruptions and thus, a matter of national security.

As such, Intrepid is a well-positioned domestic critical mineral producer with attractive production assets in close proximity to key U.S. growing regions. Against this backdrop, as we announced on October 26, the USDA selected our proposed sulfate of potash, or SOP, project near Carlsbad, New Mexico, for approximately $139 million and proposed matching funding through its FIELDS program. Based on current project plans, the facility would have annual production capacity of approximately 220,000 tons. If constructed, it would introduce a new product to our portfolio, complementing Trio and potash and expanding our presence in specialty fertilizer markets. This could be a pivotal project for Intrepid, allowing us to turn American minerals into a fertilizer product American farmers need.

The project is in the advanced stages of planning and evaluation but remain subject to completion of the award process, fulfillment of all applicable grant conditions, and a final investment decision, which we're currently targeting for late 2027. As we continue our evaluation, we remain focused on disciplined capital deployment and generating attractive long-term returns on invested capital. We look forward to sharing additional details as the project advances. Our operational improvements and the constructive selling price environment contributed to the solid cash flow we generated through the first 9 months of this year.

The cash flow, combined with the proceeds from the sale of our South Ranch asset in the second quarter, puts us in a financial position that gives us multiple pathways to shareholder value creation. Jason will review our capital allocation framework in more detail shortly, but I want to outline our two-pronged returns-focused strategy for deploying capital. First, we've identified several attractive organic growth opportunities within our existing asset base. We're in the final stages of evaluating capital investments designed to increase production volumes and lower unit costs across both segments. Jason will discuss the 2 principal projects we plan to pursue in 2027.

We believe these investments can generate attractive returns and support sustained growth over the next several years. Also on the organic growth front, our development partners continue to advance the Wendover Lithium project as they work to complete their definitive feasibility study. Discussions with potential off-takers are also in the advanced stages. In addition to growth investments, we're returning capital to shareholders through share repurchases. During the quarter, we repurchased shares under our $50 million share repurchase authorization. We would plan to accelerate the utilization of this program depending on how far below intrinsic value we believe our shares are trading.

While we purchased a limited number of shares in the third quarter, over the past 5 weeks, we've accelerated our repurchasing activity, bringing the total shares we bought since the end of June to approximately 88,000. Share repurchases are a core component of our returns-focused approach to capital allocation, not a residual use of cash. We'll continue to weigh every dollar of capital, whether directed to share repurchases, improvements to our existing operations, or potential new growth projects, against the returns it can generate for shareholders, with a clear priority on compounding per share value over time.

Before I turn it over to Zach, I'd like to extend a special thanks to all of our employees for the work they've led over the last couple of years. By working together, we've increased our production in both Trio and potash. We substantially reduced our cost in Trio and are working similarly on our potash cost structure. As a result of their good work, our assets are performing much better, more predictably and reliably as demonstrated by increasing levels of profitability over the last several quarters. I'll close by noting the 3 pillars I outlined earlier, execution, opportunity, and capital discipline are converging into a cohesive value creation framework for Intrepid.

We're making good progress formulating that framework, and we see an opportunity to generate significant returns on invested capital through organic growth investment, share repurchases, and operational execution. As that work matures, we look forward to sharing more detail with you over the coming quarters. Now I'll turn the call over to Zach for a closer look at demand, pricing and the market outlook for potash and Trio.

Looking ahead, we are monitoring factors that could tighten the supply/demand balance in early 2027. In particular, congestion at Baltic ports is currently constraining exports from Russia and Belarus. If these shipping constraints persist into next year, they could limit available supply and provide further support for the market. We are also monitoring reports that negotiations have started on the next annual potash contract in China, where another early settlement could support continued shipment activity and help keep global supply and demand balances tight. Global sulfur supply constraints are contributing to higher input costs for some sulfate of potash producers, putting pressure on operating rates and availability. A tighter market for low-chloride potassium fertilizers could support demand for Trio.

With sulfur constraints extending beyond sulfate of potash to other sulfur-containing fertilizers, Trio's sulfate sulfur component provides an attractive value proposition for growers heading into spring. Trio is a unique product that supplies 3 essential plant nutrients, low-chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfate in a naturally occurring mineral. Current supply conditions could enhance the appeal of that combination. Importantly, the sulfur in Trio occurs naturally within the langbeinite mineral we mine and is immediately available to the plants in the sulfate form. We do not need to purchase sulfur feedstock to produce Trio, reducing our exposure to the feedstock constraints affecting some other fertilizer producers.

We believe this positions Trio well to serve growers seeking low chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfur nutrition. Looking ahead to spring 2027, grower sentiment has improved although elevated input costs continue to encourage disciplined purchase decisions. Demand will be subject to regional and seasonal variation but we believe growers remain focused on maximizing yields and making effective nutrient investments. Against that backdrop, we expect continued healthy fertilizer demand through the first half of 2027. With that market context, I'll turn the call over to Rick to discuss our operating performance and the initiatives supporting our increased production outlook.

Richard Kim: Thanks, Zach. I'll focus on the operating improvements behind our third quarter production gains and the work underway to improve reliability, efficiency, and unit costs across our operations. At our potash operations, we are focused on continuing to increase production while maintaining spending discipline. On a year-to-date basis, we have held total spending approximately flat while increasing output allowing us to spread fixed costs across more tons resulting in lower unit production costs. In our HB Mine, improvements in pond management and mill recovery have contributed to increases in production volume. These changes are helping us recover additional product that otherwise would have been lost as waste.

We deliberately delayed the start of the harvest season at Moab to allow additional evaporation in our ponds. After evaluating several operating scenarios, we determined that this timing would better support long-term production by adding more tons of inventory. While this decision reduced third quarter production, we expect to recover those tons by year-end. We also expect the additional evaporation to support higher production at Moab in 2027 and a corresponding reduction in unit costs. Decisions like this reflect our focus on optimizing performance across our operations. Turning to our Trio segment. Production increased 19% year-over-year during the third quarter, driven largely by continued improvements in operating performance at the East mine.

Our team is increasing equipment availability, reducing downtime and improving productivity. Year-over-year, operating hours increased by 5%, while tons per operating hour increased by approximately 20%. We believe these improvements provide a sustainable foundation for further production growth. Higher production improved operating leverage and contributed to a 13% year-over-year reduction in cost of goods sold per ton. Together with higher realized selling prices, these improvements supported stronger segment gross margin. As Kevin noted, we are increasing our full year 2026 Trio production guidance by 10,000 tons. Our focus is on sustaining these gains while continuing to improve reliability, productivity, and unit costs. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jason to review our third quarter financial results and outlook.

Jason Tremblay: Thank you, Rick. Third quarter sales from continuing operations were roughly flat with the prior year quarter at $51 million. Gross margin from continuing operations was also in line with last year's third quarter at $10 million. Net income from continuing operations improved to $1.7 million or $0.13 per diluted share from $700,000 or $0.05 per diluted share last year. Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations increased to $11.7 million from $10.7 million last year. As a reminder, the third quarter is typically 1 of our seasonally weakest quarters, given that it follows the spring planting season and precedes the fall fertilizer application season. In the Trio segment, sales increased to $19.1 million from $18.1 million in the prior year quarter.

Sales volumes were flat, while average net realized selling price increased 1.5%. Most notably, Trio gross margin increased 33% year-over-year, driven by the positive impact of a 13,000 ton increase in production volume, which improved absorption and reduced Trio's cost of goods sold per ton, as well as favorable product mix. In Potash, segment sales were $31.3 million compared with $32.5 million in the prior year quarter. Sales volumes declined to 59,000 tons from 62,000 tons, while average net realized sales price increased 3.4% to $394 per ton. Production volume declined 17%. As Rick discussed earlier, we made a strategic decision to delay the start-up of our Moab facility following the summer evaporation process to support production levels and efficiency.

Potash segment gross margin declined due to higher COGS per ton, reflecting a production mix weighted more heavily toward Intrepid's higher cost sites as compared to last year's third quarter. Moving to cash flow and liquidity. Year-to-date cash flow from continuing operations was $50.5 million compared with $37.3 million in the prior year, with the increase partly attributable to improved operating performance. Capital spending remained disciplined with $11.3 million invested in the third quarter and $24.9 million year-to-date. We ended the third quarter with $152.3 million in cash and cash equivalents, $9.1 million in short-term investments and no debt.

As part of our capital allocation framework, we invested $14.5 million in short and long-term investments during the third quarter to earn additional returns on cash we've set aside to support our long-term balance sheet strength. Going forward, we'll continue to manage our liquidity carefully, balancing opportunities to earn returns on our cash with seasonal working capital needs investments in our growth projects and ongoing share repurchases. As Kevin mentioned, our balanced approach to capital allocation prioritizes a safe and reliable operations balance sheet flexibility and investments evaluated against the risk-adjusted return potential, execution readiness, and strategic fit. Within this framework, we will also return capital to shareholders.

As I discussed during last quarter's call, balance sheet preservation is the foundation of our capital allocation strategy. We plan to maintain approximately $50 million in liquidity to navigate cyclical downturns plus roughly $35 million for working capital needs and cash flow variability. Beyond these amounts, we will deploy capital through disciplined growth investments, particularly within our existing operating footprint and share repurchases. As Kevin indicated, we have increased our repurchase activity over the past several weeks. Since the Board approved the $50 million authorization in June, we repurchased 88,000 shares for a total of $3 million. Turning to growth investments.

Our planned spending in 2027 will focus on Trio production growth and potash mine development within our existing asset base. These investments are designed to increase production, extend the life of existing operations, and enhance the business' long-term earnings potential. The Trio and Potash investments I'll discuss are separate from the proposed SOP project, Kevin outlined. As we continue evaluating that opportunity ahead of a final investment decision, we remain committed to our broader capital allocation priorities and will assess the project within the same disciplined returns-focused framework. For Trio, we plan to invest approximately $16 million in 2027 as part of a broader initiative to increase annual production by approximately 30,000 tons above the first half 2026 run rates.

We expect this initiative to generate an internal rate of return of approximately 30%. We anticipate realizing some of the production benefits in late 2026 and expect full year 2027 Trio production in the range of 320,000 to 330,000 tons. We believe there is potential to increase annual Trio production by an additional 100,000 tons with modest incremental investment beyond 2027. For Potash, we plan to invest approximately $20 million in mine development in 2027 to sustain annual production at levels approximately 20,000 to 30,000 tons above prior years, with expected rates of return of approximately 30%. To support these initiatives, we are increasing our full year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to approximately $45 million from approximately $40 million previously.

In summary, we executed well during the third quarter, making meaningful progress toward our stated goals. We increased Trio production and significantly improved the segment's margins. Our strong balance sheet and disciplined capital allocation strategy position us to invest in organic growth while returning capital to shareholders through opportunistic share repurchases. Collectively, we expect these efforts to create long-term value for our shareholders. Operator, we are now ready to begin the Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Lucas Beaumont with UBS.

Lucas Beaumont: Just wanted to start on Trio. So I mean, pricing is up 25% or so over the last 2 years, I mean, probably half of that sort of came before the sort of more recent disruptions to the sulfur markets. So I just kind of wanted to get your view on, I guess, how would you sort of frame that in terms of what do you see as sort of temporary pricing uplift there versus what's been more structurally driven by the supply/demand setup.

So I guess as we sort of go forward and then see a normalization in those temporary factors, how much of that would you sort of expect to sort of roll off versus sort of being supported on an underlying basis?

Zachry Adams: Lucas, thank you for the question. In regards to Trio pricing and the changes we've seen over the last several years, we would assign that to a structural change. And yes, the global disruptions to sulfur are supporting that now, but on a broader level, there is just a greater awareness and recognition of magnesium and sulfur needs increasing over time in soil nutrient levels. And in combination with that as well is we're seeing a greater appreciation for the low-chloride content of Trio as well in specialty crop. So it's really all 3 components: the low-chloride potassium, the magnesium and the sulfur all having broader awareness and recognition that's helping to structurally change that price dynamic.

Kevin Crutchfield: The other thing I'd add too, Lucas, is given the conflict in the Mid East, I mean that's obviously provided some underfooting for higher sulfur prices. And to the extent that, that gets resolved tomorrow, it's not going to come back quickly. We don't think just based on the level of infrastructure damage that's been done across the system. So you can refer to it as temporary, if you want, but our view is that it's going to take a long time to get that anywhere back to normal.

Lucas Beaumont: Great. And then I guess just on the potash side, considering the markets that have been fairly balanced through the middle part of the year here, and you're kind of expecting pricing to sort of be flat to kind of slightly lower end of the fourth quarter sequentially. So I guess, how do you sort of see the set up there for market momentum for potash into the fall and then peak spring demand. I mean, you sort of see the market as tight enough that we should see pricing move higher into the spring? Or kind of what's your view currently?

Zachry Adams: Lucas, regarding the potash market, we see that as very constructive. To your point, it has been balanced throughout the year, but as we enter the fourth quarter here, there's several things going on globally. One is the reengagement of the Chinese on their next potash contract, which could drive kind of shipments to continue to be at very ratable heavy clip what we've done year-to-date. And the other more, I'd say, thing we're watching even closer is the disruption to the ports in the Baltic. Lucas Beaumont: And then I guess just on your production improvement initiatives there for next year, I mean, that's fairly substantial again as well. Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, Lucas. Good question. So on Potash and Trio, I mean the investments are different, obviously, I think on Trio, rather than talking about anything specifically we're going to do -- we just want to talk about the Trio product as a system from the mine face continuous miner shuttle cars, belt, plant infrastructure, yields, et cetera. We just -- we think there are opportunities to improve operating run time, maintenance downtime, mill throughput, yields, et cetera. And that monies -- those monies will go into just generally, I would describe as system improvements to generate better volumes over time. And it's not a sort of a onetime thing. We think that's a sustainable long-term run rate.

And we think there's upside potential beyond that which is premature to get into today. So that's kind of how we think about Trio. I'm not going to talk much more about what 1 miner does or whatever. We're just going to talk about it as improvements to the system and continuing to debottleneck the system to generate better production over time. And then on the Potash side, it's an investment that is developmental in nature to replace tons as they fall off over the future, but it will stimulate production 20,000 to 30,000 tons. We'll start to realize that next year. And look, I'd also point out, too, that some context here is important.

When we -- when you look at the numbers we've provided in terms of next year's range of guidance. You're in the mid 600,000 ton range. And it's been, I don't know, a decade or so since the company has achieved anywhere near that. And so I think that's an important part of the story that's not getting captured appropriately. And those gains have largely come over the last 2.5 or 3 years. And I'd like to credit the team that we have in place and the good work that's being done at the site level to generating those positive outcomes. I'll refer to Jason for any sort of remarks around the cost piece.

Jason Tremblay: Yes. So on the cost front. These are -- I would call them marginal tons, right? So I think what you get is much of your fixed cost isn't going to adjust. There's some amount of investment in fixed cost that come. Majority of this is marginal production with marginal costs being added. As a result, you see a pretty -- we're a high fixed cost business and you see that benefit come through. That answer is very specific to Trio and I'll get into the Potash side. But on the Trio side, you should see cost benefits just through absorption.

As we come to the Potash side, I think if you look at it on any individual mine, you're going to see cost benefits of these investments, right? So -- and largely, what this mine development does is provide higher grade to the facilities, which drives kind of more efficient production. Really, your costs aren't changing much. You're handling the same volume of raw materials to produce incremental volume. So you're getting better volume for largely similar cost structure at most of that -- at the sites.

The thing that gets hard is -- and Q3 is a good example of that, is depending which site we're producing tons at and where the relative cost positions are, you can get unusual movement in the consolidated result, right? And that's something we're going to expand on more as we move into the future and just help make sure that we help the investors and understand kind of the relative cost performance of site because I think that's a big driver that moves pieces around. But what we do know is each of our sites should see cost improvement as the mine development takes hold and the production improves.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line Vincent Andrews with Morgan Stanley.

Justin Pellegrino: This is Justin Pellegrino on for Vincent. My first question is about Trio production. And if you just annualize 2H '26 Trio production. It implies about 332,000 tons of production at today's rates which -- that's above the 2027 production guidance. So 2 questions there. Does the '27 production guidance includes some conservatism? Or do you guys expect current rates to kind of come down a little bit maybe? And then likewise, does the '27 production guidance include any additional tons from the $16 million that you plan to invest in '27?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, there's a lot in that question. So out of the $16 million that we called out, we're going to spend -- start spending a little bit of that this year. That's why we raised our capital guide a little bit. You're right, the run rate of late has been really solid but it's dangerous to annualize a quarter. So what we're trying to do is build sustainable run rates that are reliable, predictable, and dependable just like I've been saying for the last few years. So a piece of that is, is there upside in that?

Absolutely, because the team there is -- they've become very dedicated to thinking about the Trio production system as just that a system and just debottlenecking kind of weak point by weak point by weak point. And every time you do that, you generate better volumes over time. So we still think there's tremendous upside potential left on the Trio side. And we'll continue to update it on a quarterly basis. Anything you'd add?

Jason Tremblay: Yes. The only thing I'd add to that is just to your -- the first part of your answer when you were talking about -- it's dangerous to annualize a quarter. You have to keep in mind, right, there is scheduled downtime required for our assets for major maintenance. We have to take turnaround activities on specific assets and timing of those matter, right?

And so in the second half here, we're lighter on the maintenance front and lighter in terms of major asset maintenance, which is why you're seeing a higher run rate, but it's also indicative of the fact that we can run at higher rates but that's why I think you're seeing kind of a change in guide.

Justin Pellegrino: Understood, and that's much appreciated. And then the next -- I know this is kind of trying to isolate 2027 and investments happen at different points throughout the year. But if we simply just add the $16 million of Trio and $20 million that you called out in Potash to the $45 million of guidance, you get to somewhere in the $80 million ballpark of CapEx 2027. So I was just hoping you could maybe help us figure out if that's in the right ballpark. I know you had mentioned previously some maybe larger sustaining CapEx items as well in '27. So just any kind of help us triangulate where 2027 CapEx could land?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. I'll take the initial part of that, Jason, will probably have some color to add. But if you imputed that the way you just described, you'd be too high. So yes, we did this year from -- I mean, we started, I think, the year $45 million, we moved it down $40 million. But the addition of those 2 numbers is not going to get you close to what we're talking about for sustaining. Next year, it will be south of that.

Jason Tremblay: The only thing I'd add, Justin, to that, just context-wise, right, we do mine development activity every year, right? So we just want to make sure people understand these are being done with a return focus, right? Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jason Ursaner with Bumbershoot Holdings.

Jason Ursaner: Sorry, I was on mute. Just on the Trio on the additional tons for next year and then kind of this road map for maybe additional 100,000 tons with moderate investment from there. Has that changed at all the marketability between the granular standard and fine langbeinite? Like are you adding any way to get additional tons of one? Or is it just kind of across the board?

Zachry Adams: Jason, thanks for the question. This is Zach. As we think about the additional tons of Trio, we see that growth coming from a variety of areas. First is focus on specialty crops like we talked about earlier and also where we see crops and soil types that have a broader recognition of sulfur and magnesium needs. And then with that growth, we see that as a combination of both market expansion and share gains. And within that, that expansion, that's geographically as well as customer base and also crop based, and we're currently working through and putting together plans for what that will look like into next year and beyond.

Kevin Crutchfield: And to the extent that the SOP project proceeds, that will be a source as well, as opposed to trying to find new markets in the U.S. or trying to grab market share or whatever. So that will be an outlet as well. To the extent the project proceeds.

Jason Ursaner: So for the SOP project, is it -- would you be using some of the standard and fine langbeinite as a raw input and then you don't have to market kind of the less desirable lower margin langbeinite because you could use that to create SOP, you could sell the higher margin granular and then kind of -- you have sort of an exchange reaction instead of a Mannheim process so you could get SOP and then also have mag chloride?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. No Mannheim process required here because we already have the sulfur on site. So the answer to your question is generally yes. That's how we're thinking about it, and that's how it work.

Jason Ursaner: Okay. Does it kind of increase your desire or willingness to try to expand the Trio production and have more of the standard and fine product, if you have an outlet for it, I guess, is what I'm eventually trying to get to?

Zachry Adams: Jason yes, absolutely. Absolutely. SOP drives the ability for us to grow our Trio production significantly more than it is today with providing a nice premium outlet for those fines into an upgraded specialty fertilizer product.

Jason Ursaner: Okay. And then, I guess, just a broader question for Kevin. You -- around $400 million market cap, $160 million of cash, you still have the $50 million eventually coming from Exxon. So it's around $190 million, $200 million of enterprise value just based on trailing numbers of EBITDA. I mean you're kind of trading 3.5x EBITDA or so. So the implication at least to me is either EBITDA is unsustainable, you're at some cyclical peak, you're structurally not converting EBITDA cash and none of those sound at all kind of what you're saying, which is pretty upbeat, optimistic and anything. So I guess from your perspective, what are -- I guess, what are people sort of missing here?

And what is going to change that in people's mind eventually for this being not only a sustainable business, but kind of an improving 1 pretty significantly is what it sounds like.

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, that's an excellent question. I mean the way I think about it is start with the core assets. And we've been pounding the table for -- ever since I've been here about laser focus on core assets, getting them running better on an improved basis, more consistent, more reliable. And I think by any metric you look at over the last 2 to 4 years, that's a -- or a green check mark in that box. And then over time, too, the other thing that's happened is as we've continued to survey the asset base, you've got some new eyes looking at things here and there.

We're coming up with a lot of internal organic growth opportunities that we think are very investable that will have very nice returns on them. So I think you're right. I think maybe we're not telling the story, right? But this is a story of a very nice turnaround over a 2-, 3-year period with a lot of upside potential in the future. Now baseline with all that is we have to execute. We have to continue to do that quarter after quarter after quarter to regain sort of that credibility and that track record. But we think that there's tremendous upside here.

And I'm not going to speak to the share buying program exactly, but we upped our purchases when we saw weakness in the stock. And I think you could expect that to continue if you continue to see weakness in the stock because we think there's upside value here and it's a good value. So if a little frustration is coming through in my voice, should be, because I am a little bit but I also take the responsibility that we've got to tell the story better and make the value proposition more clear going forward because there's tremendous upside here.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Vitaly Kononov with Freedom Capital Markets.

Vitaly Kononov: So I'd like to maybe dissect on the cost divergence in the 2 segments. So we saw a year-over-year increase in Potash and year-over-year decrease in Trio. So maybe you can distinguish the factors that are driving the increase in Potash and explain some of the efficiency gains that helped to bring the cost of Trio down?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. Look, on the Trio side, as I mentioned earlier, that's an underground mine. We have continuous miner sections operating underground. The continuous miner loads coal into a shuttle cars, shuttle cars takes it to the belt. The belt takes it outside. We process it through the plant, and generate a salable product. All of that is a system. And what we've been doing is, as I said earlier, debottlenecking that system. Part of the problem early on was we had some continuous mining units that were older and experiencing low reliability, low availability, et cetera. So we replaced those, and that enhanced the system. But what it does is it points out, you've got a bottleneck somewhere else.

So we're just moving constraint to constraint across the site, and what that's led to is more operating time, higher productivity, more bits on langbeinite time in the face. The mill is operating really well. Our yields are higher, we're staying in the ore zone better. So all that has contributed to better production and better fixed cost absorption over the last couple of years. And I think the exciting thing about it is this is not the eighth inning of a ninth inning ball game, we're probably in the fourth inning here, on this thing. So I think it's got more runway, and we're excited to pursue it.

We're being very thoughtful about it because markets are somewhat fixed in the U.S., and we've got to think about proper outlets, and not destroying economic value as it relates to the value of the product in the marketplace. But we expect us to be very thoughtful around that approach over the next 2, 3 years but we're super excited about what that potential runway looks like.

Jason Tremblay: If I could add, Vitaly, just on your question on the Potash side. So -- the interesting part and the difference is, in Trio, we're ramping up one facility. So the cost performance is really visible based on kind of ramping that production and seeing the unit cost improvements for that facility. In Potash, right, we've got 3 facilities, and the production increases this year, the production improvement this year because we are improving production year-over-year in this year, but the improvements this year have largely been at 2 of our mines, HB and Wendover which are a higher cost facility than Moab, which is the third facility.

And so our production growth is happening at the 2 higher cost facilities. But at the same time, though, the cost per ton at those facilities is improving. And so the whole idea here for us is improved production at all of our facilities and drive better results. It doesn't show up in that consolidated cost per ton or COGS per ton measure because of that product mix. And that's what we've been trying to communicate. We are going to work and focus on better telling that story, moving into the future.

But I think what we see is improved cost performance at all the sites as the production ramps up, it's just the mix is making it difficult to see it on a consolidated level.

Vitaly Kononov: On the Wendover Lithium project, do I sense a change of sentiment here that the project could be the time lines of installing could be delayed somewhat, or am I guessing wrong?

Kevin Crutchfield: I mean relative to kind of where we started talking about this maybe a little bit, but they're still looking at definitive feasibility study by first quarter engineering continues, value-add engineering continues, FEL3 process is done, advanced discussions continue with offtake partners. That's actually going exceedingly well. So yes, but relative to maybe where we started a quarter or something, but it's not terrible, not to be unexpected in this space either.

Vitaly Kononov: All right. Got it. And the last question for me on the recent USDA announcements. I'm just curious what conditions are still remaining before the funding becomes binding? And how much customer offtake commitment would you require before approving construction?

Kevin Crutchfield: So we're just in the early stages of finalizing that work with the USDA. I suspect that will take a good bit of time. And as it relates to what we'd want to have presold before we gave the green light. I think that's part and parcel to the final investment decision process, what the markets look like, where we can move the tons, as you know, a lot of this product is an import product, which we think we could displace but that would be part of the final investment decision, along with final CapEx, what's the cost structure look like et cetera, et cetera.

So in the next -- over the course of the next 8 to 12 months, we have a lot of work to do, and we'll be able to update you in the coming quarters on how that work is shaping up.
